findings.asked: State the Principle of Moments, then apply it to a beam.
findings.wentWrong: Only the most able stated the principle fully - 'about the pivot' was usually missing; in the calculation the distances printed on the diagram were used directly instead of the distances from the pivot.
findings.rule: Every distance in a moment is measured from the pivot; work it out if the diagram gives something else.

findings.asked: State the Principle of Moments, find the size and direction of the force on a supported beam, then an unknown distance.
findings.wentWrong: Poorly attempted by most: statements omitted 'about a point' and 'when in equilibrium'; the support force came out as 5 by subtracting the two loads instead of adding them, with 'clockwise' given as its direction; finding the distance by moments was the strongest differentiator on the paper.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the full statement, added the downward forces for the upward reaction, and set clockwise moments equal to anticlockwise moments with the unknown distance as the only unknown.
findings.rule: Reaction = sum of the downward forces; then one moments equation about the pivot.

findings.asked: Direction and unit of a moment, then the distance needed to balance a beam.
findings.wentWrong: The direction and especially the unit were very poorly answered; the balancing distance (10 cm) was often right.
findings.rule: Unit: newton metre (N m) - not N/m; direction: clockwise or anticlockwise.

findings.asked: Formula and unit for the moment of a force, then a Principle of Moments calculation.
findings.wentWrong: The formula was known but the unit was often N/m or N/cm; the calculation, historically a weak area, was pleasingly well done at Higher (and still hard at Foundation).
findings.rule: Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot, in N m.

ruleToRemember: Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot, unit N m, direction clockwise or anticlockwise. Principle of Moments: when an object is in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point. The support force equals the total downward force.
aStarSignal: Finding an unknown distance or force with one moments equation about a well-chosen point, and a word-perfect principle with 'about a point' and 'in equilibrium'.
